subject: Kyllo v. United States (2001) and thermal imaging of the home / the 'general public use' Fourth Amendment rule
central_question: Can the police point a heat-sensing device at your house from a public street, with no warrant and no foot on your property, and use what it reveals against you — or is that a search of your home?
viewer_promise: By the end, the viewer understands how a single 2001 Supreme Court decision drew a 'firm but bright' line at the front door of every American home and why the standard it created — technology 'not in general public use' — governs modern surveillance of the home.
surprise: A federal agent learned what was happening inside a private home without ever touching it — just by reading the heat leaking through the walls from a car across the street — and the Supreme Court had to decide, 5-4, whether measuring that heat was a 'search.'
stakes: Whether the government needs a warrant before using sense-enhancing technology to reveal what happens inside your home, and how that 1992 heat-camera fight controls today's drones, sensors, and through-wall devices.
target_audience: English-speaking US general audience interested in law, policing, privacy, technology and how systems work
demand_evidence: 'Know your rights,' privacy, and surveillance-tech content is a large, durable YouTube genre; Kyllo is the legal floor under 'can they scan my house.'
Landmark-case explainers sustain long-tail search interest, and the surveillance-technology angle refreshes with every new sensing device.
competition: Most existing videos recite the holding or fold Kyllo into a general Fourth Amendment survey; few center the neutral 'how the general-public-use rule was built, and why it keeps moving' causal angle.
differentiation: Frames Kyllo as the moment the Court future-proofed the home against sensing technology, present-tense and self-relevant, with primary-source citations and a neutral, advertiser-safe tone. Continues the 'police vs. the privacy of the home/phone' vein.
research_feasibility: High: the opinion is public domain (533 U.S. 27); Cornell LII and Oyez provide the full opinion, syllabus, dissent and case record.
visual_feasibility: High: restrained thermal/heat-leak visualization, a cold suburban stakeout, the closed front door as 'core of the home,' a 5-4 split motif, and a modern-surveillance tie (drones/sensors).
risk_notes: Decided landmark case (2001); opinion is public domain - advertiser-friendly.
Drug-adjacent subject: the indoor marijuana grow is treated only as a heat/light source and a factual court record; no drug depiction, no how-to, no glamorization.
Danny Kyllo is a living real person on the public court record; treat respectfully and factually, by role; no real-person likeness in AI visuals (invariant 11).
Keep tone neutral between home-privacy and legitimate law-enforcement need. Do NOT overstate the holding: the Court did not ban thermal imaging; it required a warrant and remanded.
Generated visuals are illustration/reconstruction, never presented as authentic surveillance or archival footage.
kill_conditions: Cannot source the holding and key facts to the primary opinion (533 U.S. 27) plus one independent reference.
